desc:
Houses stand in a row and house i holds nums[i] coins. Robbing two neighbouring houses normally sets off the alarm, but tonight the alarm system has a single lapse: your set of robbed houses may contain at most one pair of neighbouring houses (indices i and i + 1 both robbed). Robbing three houses in a row would contain two such pairs, so it is not allowed.

Return the maximum number of coins you can collect. For example, for [5, 6, 1, 1, 5] the answer is 16 (houses 0, 1 and 4).
hints: Without the lapse this is House Robber with the two states 'last house robbed' and 'last house not robbed'. The lapse is a one-time resource, so remember whether it has been spent.
Use four running values: (last robbed or not) x (lapse used or not). Robbing right after a robbed house is the only move that spends the lapse.

With r0 = last not robbed and r1 = last robbed, and u0 / u1 for the lapse unused / used: new_free[u] = max of both options of the previous house; new_robbed[u] = free[u] + x; and new_robbed[used] also considers robbed[unused] + x.
editorial: Let s[t][u] be the best total over the processed prefix, where t = 1 if the last house is robbed and u = 1 if the lapse has already been used (a robbed pair exists). For the next house with value x: not robbing it gives s'[0][u] = max(s[0][u], s[1][u]). Robbing it after a skipped house keeps the lapse state: s'[1][u] = s[0][u] + x. Robbing it directly after a robbed house is the lapse, so s'[1][1] also considers s[1][0] + x.

From s[1][1] you cannot rob the next house, since a second pair would appear; the transitions never allow it. Start with s[0][0] = 0 and everything else impossible, and return the maximum of all four values at the end. Time O(n), space O(1). The same idea (carry a small 'how many exceptions are left' counter in the state) works for any bounded number of rule violations.
solution:
def robWithOneLapse(nums):
    NEG = -10 ** 18
    f0, f1 = 0, NEG       # last not robbed: lapse unused / used
    r0, r1 = NEG, NEG     # last robbed: lapse unused / used
    for x in nums:
        nf0 = max(f0, r0)
        nf1 = max(f1, r1)
        nr0 = f0 + x
        nr1 = max(f1 + x, r0 + x)
        f0, f1, r0, r1 = nf0, nf1, nr0, nr1
    return max(f0, f1, r0, r1)
